---
title: "Validation against R"
subtitle: "Why the numbers match, and where they do not"
---

The claim this port makes is not that it implements the same statistics as the
OHDSI R package, but that it produces the **same numbers**. This page explains
what that took and how far it holds.

## Why not just use SciPy?

The obvious implementation reaches for `scipy.optimize.minimize`,
`scipy.integrate.quad` and `numpy.random`. Doing so produces results that are
statistically equivalent and numerically different — typically in the third or
fourth decimal place, occasionally more when an optimiser lands in a different
basin.

For a package whose output is a p-value that someone will compare against 0.05,
and for a port that people will want to check against an existing R analysis,
that is not good enough. So the R-specific numerical machinery was ported
directly:

| Component | What it replaces | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `_roptim.nmmin` | `scipy.optimize.minimize(method="Nelder-Mead")` | R's Nelder–Mead uses different convergence criteria and lands 3–4 decimals away. |
| `_roptim.vmmin` | `method="BFGS"` | R's BFGS with R's finite-difference gradient (`ndeps = 1e-3`), not an analytic one. |
| `_roptim.optimhess` | `scipy` Hessian | R's finite-difference Hessian, for `estimateCovarianceMatrix=True`. |
| `_roptim.uniroot` | `scipy.optimize.brentq` | R's Brent `zeroin` with `tol = eps^0.25` — a much looser tolerance than SciPy's default. |
| `_rintegrate.integrate` | `scipy.integrate.quad` | QUADPACK at R's tolerances (`1.22e-4`), not SciPy's (`1.49e-8`). |
| `_rrng` | `numpy.random` | R's Mersenne-Twister, `set.seed` scrambling, inversion-method normals, `rpois`, `rbinom`, and `R_unif_index` rejection sampling. |
| `_rmath.dnorm/dpois/dbinom` | `scipy.stats` | R's `nmath`, including Loader's saddle-point algorithm; SciPy differs by up to 2.4e-13. |

## The gold standard

Verification is against **R 4.6.1 with EmpiricalCalibration 3.1.4**, on 56
checkpoints covering every exported function. The generator script and the
recorded values live in the repository:

```
extras/r-parity/generate_r_gold_standard.R   # run in R, writes gold.json
extras/r-parity/gold.json                    # the recorded R values
extras/r-parity/compare_to_r.py              # compares the port against them
```

## Results

| Agreement | Functions |
|---|---|
| **Bit-identical** (exactly 0 difference) | `fitNull`, `fitNullNonNormalLl`, `convertNullToErrorModel`, `computeTraditionalP`, `computeTraditionalCi`, `computeExpectedAbsoluteSystematicError`, `evaluateCiCalibration`, `compareEase`, all three `computeCv*` critical values, `simulateMaxSprtData`, the MCMC starting state, and all five packaged datasets |
| **~1e-15** | `calibrateLlr`, `computePFromLlr` / `computeLlrFromP`, `fitMcmcNull` posterior summaries, `calibrateP` under an MCMC null, the raw MaxSPRT samplers |
| **~1e-13** | `calibrateConfidenceInterval` (Brent root-finding at `tol = eps^0.25`), `simulateControls` |
| **~3e-10** | `fitSystematicErrorModel`, especially its covariance matrix |

The 3e-10 entry is the largest and has a clear cause: BFGS accumulates through
finite-difference gradients, and finite differencing amplifies last-ulp
differences in the objective by roughly `1/ndeps`. Over the iterations of a
four-parameter fit that compounds into the tenth decimal. It is not a defect in
either implementation — it is what optimisation through numerical derivatives
does with inputs that differ in their final bit.

## Random numbers

`ec.set_seed(n)` reproduces R's `set.seed(n)` stream, so stochastic functions
agree run-for-run rather than merely in distribution.

The raw draws are **bit-identical** to R's: `unif_rand`, `rpois`, `rbinom` and
`sample.int`. This is asserted directly in the test suite:

```{python}
from empiricalcalibration._rrng import RRandom

# R: set.seed(101); runif(5)
print(RRandom(101).runif(5))

# R: set.seed(123); rpois(6, 3.7)
print(RRandom(123).rpois_n(6, 3.7))

# R: set.seed(3); sample.int(45, 8, replace = TRUE)
print(RRandom(3).sample_int(45, 8))
```

Two derived quantities differ in the last bits, for reasons worth stating
precisely:

**Normal draws** differ by at most 1 ulp. R's `qnorm` uses the AS 241 rational
approximation, which rounds differently in the final bit from the port's
evaluation of the same polynomial.

**Values of the form `mu + sigma * z` or `a + (b - a) * u`** differ by ~1e-14
relative. R's C compiler contracts those expressions into a fused multiply-add
on this platform, computing them with a single rounding; NumPy rounds the
multiply and the add separately. This is why `simulateControls` appears at ~1e-13
rather than bit-identical even though its underlying uniform stream matches
exactly.

## The test suite

The suite is ported from the R package's `testthat` suite and extended with
regression tests that pin values produced by R, plus coverage of the ported
numerics, the datasets, the result classes and scalar-argument handling.

```bash
python -m pytest -q                  # everything
python -m pytest -q -m "not slow"    # skip the expensive Monte-Carlo and
                                     # non-normal-likelihood fits
```

The suite includes explicit R-parity assertions rather than only checking
statistical properties. For example:

```python
def test_fitNull_reproduces_r(sccs):
    """Bit-exact against R 4.6.1 EmpiricalCalibration 3.1.4."""
    negatives = sccs[sccs.groundTruth == 0]
    null = ec.fitNull(negatives.logRr, negatives.seLogRr)
    assert null[0] == 0.79215805192387778
    assert null[1] == 0.28343634583577032
```

Note `==` rather than `approx`: for the functions listed as bit-identical above,
any deviation at all is a regression.

## Scope of the guarantee

These comparisons were made on macOS on arm64 with a particular R and BLAS
build. The bit-identical results depend on IEEE 754 double arithmetic and on
both implementations evaluating operations in the same order, which the ports
are written to ensure. What they do not control is the platform's own
floating-point behaviour — most notably compiler contraction of multiply-add,
which is exactly the effect visible in the normal-draw discrepancy above. On a
different platform, expect the bit-identical column to become "agreeing to
~1e-15" rather than to break.

## Known deliberate differences

These are design decisions, not deviations, and are listed in full on
[Coming from R](guide/from-r.qmd#deliberate-differences): matplotlib figures
instead of ggplot objects, `cohortMethod.groundTruth` as an integer rather than
a factor, `None` defaults instead of R missing arguments, Python exceptions
instead of `stop()`, and `print()` instead of `message()`.
